title: 800 V DC: less copper, room for compute
timing_note: Dry-run allowances only; revise from actual explanation and discussion rather than filling a runtime target.
review_state: Learner-feedback revision: explicit single-phase power dips, three-pair voltage explanation, scoped converter losses and attributed architecture forecasts. Ready for the next dry run.
presentation_rules: Use one explanatory headline per slide. Show essential labels and assumptions beside the diagram; omit bottom captions and repeated takeaway slogans.
Start with a physical constraint, then build closed-circuit and waveform intuition before the copper and heat arithmetic.

Keep the 100 kW average real-power anchor visible through DC, single-phase AC and balanced three-phase AC. Distinguish instantaneous power from its cycle average; introduce losses at an explicit boundary change.
On current, conductor-loss, and conversion-loss steps, ask for a prediction before revealing the result.
Use the same load and diagram positions throughout the architecture sequence; change conversion placement deliberately.
Architecture drawings show selected functional boundaries. They are conceptual schematics, not wiring diagrams.
Keep equal conductor geometry visible in the copper scene. Equal effective resistance in the heat model is a separate idealization.
Compute displayed answers with the tested three-phase AC and two-wire DC model rather than embedding numbers in generated illustrations.
Hold receiving-end real power fixed within each declared comparison. State AC line-to-line RMS voltage, power factor and resistance per conductor.
Distinguish three claims: copper under equal geometry; space under a specified equipment placement; input energy under a complete loss balance.
Finish by resolving the architecture question. Add an exercise only when it advances the engineering reasoning.

steps.title: How can 800 V DC reduce copper and free compute-rack space?
steps.headline: How can 800 V DC reduce copper and free compute-rack space?
notes: Goal: less distribution copper; more compute-rack space.
Anchor: 100 kW received by the load, averaged over an electrical cycle.
First: closed circuits, alternating current, then three phases.
Keep material, equipment space and energy efficiency as separate questions.
steps.cue: Point to the 100 kW load; introduce the supply labels as the question the next scenes will explain.
explanation: The design ambition is more usable compute power with less distribution copper and less compute-rack space occupied by power-conversion equipment. Hall-space benefits depend on where that equipment moves.

Keep one reference visible: the load receives 100 kW of average real power. First establish how a closed circuit delivers energy, what changes with alternating current and why three phases can use three current-carrying conductors. Then compare 480 V three-phase AC with 800 V DC.

The introductory waveforms use equivalent resistive loads chosen to receive the same average power. They explain electrical quantities; they do not represent rack power electronics or establish that the same equipment can accept each supply directly. Conductor and converter losses enter explicitly in later scenes.

steps.title: A closed DC circuit carries current to the load and back.
steps.headline: A closed DC circuit carries current to the load and back.
steps.cue: Trace the complete loop through source, load and return; distinguish current direction from delivered power.
notes: Voltage: energy per unit charge. Current: charge passing per second.
Steady DC here: fixed polarity; conventional current keeps one direction around the loop.
800 V across the load × 125 A through it = 100 kW.
Outgoing and return each carry 125 A; do not add them as 250 A of delivered current.
Ideal wires for now; protective earth is not the normal return conductor.
explanation: A voltage is an electrical potential difference: energy per unit charge. Current measures the rate at which charge passes a point. A source, a load and a complete conducting loop allow current to flow. The load receives electrical energy while charge continues around the circuit; the load does not consume the charge.

In this steady DC model, the source maintains a fixed polarity and 800 V across the load. Conventional current travels from the positive supply connection, through the load, and back through the return conductor. Both conductors carry 125 A as parts of the same loop. Adding their current magnitudes would count the same circuit current twice.

The received power is P = V × I = 800 × 125 = 100,000 W, or 100 kW. It is constant in this model. Direct current need not always have constant magnitude; steady values are the deliberate simplification here. Protective earth is not the normal load-current return.

The waveform primer assumes ideal conductors and no converters. At this boundary, source power equals received power. Later scenes add resistance and conversion losses rather than silently changing this energy balance.

steps.title: Single-phase AC makes this load’s power dip twice per cycle.
steps.headline: Single-phase AC makes this load’s power dip twice per cycle.
steps.cue: Follow the current reversal, then pause at a zero crossing: received power dips to zero. Ask what three staggered phases would change.
notes: Single-phase teaching model: voltage and current reverse together through an ideal resistive load.
Instantaneous power = voltage × current; two negative signs still give positive received power.
RMS: same resistive heating as a DC value; 480 V RMS is about 679 V peak for a sine wave.
208.3 A RMS here; received power swings 0–200 kW but averages 100 kW.
This resistive example has power factor 1; real rack electronics need a separate model.
The actual data-hall comparison is three-phase. The dip belongs to this ideal load model; it does not mean a real server switches off at every zero crossing.
explanation: The load is the equipment receiving power. Here it is modeled as an ideal resistance so the waveform arithmetic is transparent. A 480 V single-phase load can be supplied between two phases of a three-phase system; the voltage label alone does not specify the number of phases. This introductory circuit is not the three-phase data-hall feeder used in the later comparison.

Start with one sinusoidal AC source and a resistive load. The voltage changes polarity every half-cycle. The current also reverses, in step with the voltage. With voltage and current referenced consistently at the receiving load, instantaneous power is their product: p(t) = v(t) × i(t). During the negative half-cycle both signs reverse, so the load continues receiving positive power. Alternating current does not imply that this load returns all the delivered energy every half-cycle. The slider uses a 60 Hz example: 60 complete cycles per second, or about 16.7 milliseconds per cycle. Changing frequency changes that period; the power reasoning shown here still applies to the ideal resistive load.

An AC value must say whether it is a peak or an effective value. RMS means root mean square: square the waveform, average over a cycle, then take the square root. A given RMS current produces the same average heating in the same resistance as that numerical DC current. For a sine wave, peak = √2 × RMS; 480 V RMS therefore has a peak of about 679 V.

Choose this illustrative single-phase load to receive the same 100 kW average power. At 480 V RMS, its current is 100,000/480 = 208.33 A RMS. Voltage and current are sinusoidal and in phase, so power factor is one. Its instantaneous received power is p(θ) = 200 sin²(θ) kW: zero at the waveform crossings, 200 kW at the peaks, and 100 kW averaged over a complete cycle.

The average remains the comparison anchor even though instantaneous power changes. Over one hour at this operating point, the load receives 100 kWh, just as the preceding ideal DC load does. This single-phase case explains the waveform; the data-hall comparison will use balanced three-phase AC. Actual rack power electronics are not resistors and can change current waveforms and power factor.

steps.title: Three balanced phases fill the power dips of a single phase.
steps.headline: Three balanced phases fill the power dips of a single phase.
steps.cue: Scrub the cycle: follow one phase, then combine all three. Contrast the sum of currents with the sum of received powers.
notes: Three equal AC phases, shifted by 120°: one-third of a cycle.
Balanced wye teaching load: three equal resistive branches meet at a common star point.
Each branch averages 33.3 kW; staggered power pulses add to 100 kW at every instant.
The three line currents sum to zero: other phases complete the return path.
No neutral load current only in this balanced sinusoidal model; real systems may need a neutral.
explanation: Three-phase AC uses three sinusoidal phase voltages of equal magnitude, offset from one another by 120 degrees, or one-third of a cycle. For this teaching model, connect three equal resistive load branches at a shared star point, called a wye connection. A phase conductor connects to the other end of each branch.

Keep the total average received power at 100 kW. Each branch averages one-third of that, about 33.3 kW. Its instantaneous power rises and falls between zero and about 66.7 kW. Because the three waveforms are staggered, their instantaneous powers add to a constant 100 kW in this balanced sinusoidal model. A moment of zero voltage on one phase is not a moment of zero total power.

The three signed line currents also add to zero at every instant, but that statement concerns charge flow, not power. Current entering the load through some phase conductors leaves through the others; their roles vary over the cycle. A neutral conductor between the source neutral and load star point would carry zero load current in this ideal balanced case, so the normal load-current circuit can operate with three phase conductors.

Zero neutral current is conditional on this balanced sinusoidal model. Unequal loads and nonlinear current waveforms can require a neutral; protection and grounding requirements also remain. The later copper comparison counts three AC phase conductors under the stated idealization, not every conductor required in every real installation.

The DC, single-phase AC and three-phase AC examples all deliver 100 kW on average. DC is steady in its introductory model, single-phase resistive power pulsates, and the three-phase total is steady under balanced conditions. None of the three phases creates extra energy.

Constant aggregate instantaneous power in this model is a waveform property. It is not a claim that three phases create redundant feeds or guarantee reliability. A real rectifier load can have different current waveforms.

steps.title: 480 V is the voltage between two live phase conductors.
steps.headline: 480 V is the voltage between two live phase conductors.
steps.cue: Identify both meter probes, then open Why not 960 V? and move through a cycle.
notes: Voltage is always measured between two points.
L1, L2 and L3 are all live phases; the meter probes L1 and L2.
The other pairs L2–L3 and L3–L1 also measure 480 V RMS in this balanced system.
In a 480Y/277 V wye system, phase-to-neutral is about 277 V; neutral is distinct from protective earth.
Compare the pair waveforms: equal RMS magnitude, different timing. Add signed values at the same instant, not the RMS labels.
explanation: L1, L2 and L3 are three live phase conductors. Neither of the two meter connections is ground. In the balanced system, any phase pair measures 480 V RMS: L1–L2, L2–L3 or L3–L1. Voltage uses two measurement points even when the system has three phases. Neutral and protective earth have distinct roles; they are not an unmentioned third phase.

The 480 V label is an RMS value over a cycle, not a constant signed voltage difference. Instantaneous differences obey v12 + v23 + v31 = 0. Their waveforms are shifted in time, so the RMS magnitudes cannot be added as 480 + 480. For example, at one instant phase-to-neutral voltages are about +392, −196 and −196 V: the three signed pair differences are about +588, 0 and −588 V. Each pair still measures 480 V RMS over a full cycle.

In the data-hall comparison, 480 V AC means the RMS voltage measured between two phase conductors: line-to-line voltage. It is not the voltage across each branch of the wye teaching load. Each branch sees the phase-to-neutral voltage, measured from its phase conductor to the star point. In a balanced system that RMS value is 480/√3 ≈ 277.1 V.

Line-to-line voltage is the instantaneous difference between two phase voltages. Those equal sine waves are separated by 120 degrees, so the difference has √3 times the magnitude of either phase voltage. This is why the conversion uses √3; treating each branch as a separate 480 V load would mix measurement conventions.

Add the three branch powers. With sinusoidal currents in phase with their respective phase voltages, total real power is P = 3 × V_phase-to-neutral,RMS × I_line,RMS. Substitute V_phase-to-neutral = V_line-to-line/√3 to obtain P = √3 × V_line-to-line,RMS × I_line,RMS. More generally, balanced three-phase real power includes a power-factor multiplier, PF: real power divided by apparent power. The ideal resistive model uses PF = 1.

At 100 kW and 480 V line-to-line RMS, each line carries 100,000/(√3 × 480) = 120.281 A RMS. The corresponding 800 V DC example carries 100,000/800 = 125 A in each of its two conductors. The current magnitudes are close because the AC formula uses three phases and a line-to-line voltage convention. The voltage labels alone do not specify equal circuit arrangements.

The single-phase primer at 480 V RMS used a different arrangement and therefore required 208.33 A RMS for the same average power. It is not the baseline for the copper comparison. From the next scene onward, compare 480 V balanced three-phase AC with 800 V two-wire DC at the same 100 kW receiving-end power; introduce conductor resistance only when calculating heat.

steps.title: Two DC conductors use one-third less copper than three equal AC conductors.
steps.headline: Two DC conductors use one-third less copper than three equal AC conductors.
steps.cue: Show three equal AC conductors beside two DC conductors, then continue to the non-obvious current comparison.
notes: Equal length, cross-section and copper material for every conductor.
Copper mass ∝ conductor count × length × cross-section: two pieces versus three.
2/3 as much copper → 33.3% less; a material comparison.
Cable capacity unproven; equal effective resistance is a separate assumption.
explanation: For equal conductor length L, cross-sectional area A and copper density, mass is proportional to count × L × A. Three AC conductors versus two DC conductors therefore gives a DC/AC copper ratio of 2/3: 33.3% less current-carrying conductor copper at the stated equal 100 kW load.

This excludes protective earth, any neutral, insulation and terminations. It compares material quantity; it does not establish an ampacity-qualified installation. The later equal-effective-resistance heat calculation is a separate idealization.
The ambition is more power with less material. This controlled comparison establishes the material arithmetic first; it does not yet establish safe additional power capacity.

steps.title: The same 100 kW needs nearly the same current in each conductor.
steps.headline: The same 100 kW needs nearly the same current in each conductor.
notes: DC: I = P/V. Balanced three-phase AC: I = P/(√3 × V_line-to-line × PF).
At 100 kW: 480 V AC → 120.3 A RMS per line; 800 V DC → 125 A per conductor.
DC current is slightly higher here; fewer conductors explain the copper reduction.
Raise DC voltage → lower DC current. Later scenes reset to 800 V.
steps.cue: Ask whether fewer conductors means less current per conductor. Reveal, then move the DC voltage slider.
explanation: For DC, I = P/V. For balanced three-phase AC, I = P/(√3 × V_line-to-line × PF). At 100 kW, 480 V AC and PF = 1 give 120.3 A per line; 800 V DC gives 125 A per conductor.
Two instead of three is 33.3% less conductor copper under the preceding geometry assumptions, not 33.3% less current. The DC voltage slider changes only this scene; later comparisons return to 800 V.

steps.title: Two DC conductors produce 28% less heat in this comparison.
steps.headline: Two DC conductors produce 28% less heat in this comparison.
notes: Same copper resistivity, length and area: equal 10 mΩ effective resistance per conductor is the heat-model assumption.
DC produces 28% less conductor heat, not 28% lower conductivity.
The difference is about 122 W at 100 kW delivered; this is not a 28% facility-energy saving.
steps.cue: Ask how to total the heating across all wires, then reveal.
explanation: At equal resistance R per conductor, total feeder heat is 3I_AC²R for balanced three-phase AC and 2I_DC²R for two-wire DC. With R = 0.01 Ω, the losses are about 434.0 W and 312.5 W respectively.

The DC-to-AC heat ratio is 0.72: 28% less conductor heat. Equal effective resistance is an additional model assumption, not an automatic consequence of equal copper geometry. The earlier 33.3% figure described material; neither number is a whole-facility saving.

Conductivity is the material property; it has not changed here. The difference is about 122 W, or 0.12% of the 100 kW delivered load. The local heating comparison helps explain conductor count, but cannot establish an architecture-wide efficiency gain.

steps.title: Stepping down AC first lets established equipment supply the 800 V DC bus.
steps.headline: Stepping down AC first lets established equipment supply the 800 V DC bus.
steps.cue: Trace the supply through the transformer and electronic converter. Use Converter losses to account for heat in the electronic stage.
notes: Transformer: AC voltage reduction and isolation, using windings and a magnetic core.
Electronic converter: lower-voltage AC input, controlled 800 V DC output.
This route uses established component types; direct MV products exist but are a developing data-center alternative.
In Converter losses, count only the electronic supply: 98% efficiency is assumed; the upstream transformer is outside this calculation.
explanation: This supply path combines established transformer and low-voltage power-electronic technologies. Direct medium-voltage conversion for an 800 V data-center supply is a developing alternative, not an unavailable one: Eaton currently lists a medium-voltage solid-state transformer with an 800 V DC output. A product listing does not establish widespread deployment or a universal economic advantage.

A conventional transformer has conductive windings around a magnetic core, commonly laminated steel. Alternating current in a winding creates changing magnetic flux that induces voltage in another winding. It does not need a permanent magnet or electronic switching to perform this function. Natural convection can remove its heat; some larger transformer designs use fans. The heat view here instead isolates the electronic AC/DC converter downstream of the transformer.

The reason for conventional step-down is practical: medium-voltage insulation and voltage transformation are handled by the transformer, leaving lower-voltage power electronics to rectify and regulate the output. Direct medium-voltage conversion is possible, but changes the semiconductor, voltage-sharing, insulation, protection and control problem. Scarcity of high-voltage switching devices can make that solution more complex; it is not a rule that rectification stops working above 10 kV.

The earlier SemiAnalysis quotation appears in “Medium Voltage Rectifiers: Is There Room for Everyone?”. Its following discussion expressly acknowledges medium-voltage rectifiers using series-stacked silicon devices. Read the passage as a commercialization and topology tradeoff, rather than a universal ban on medium-voltage rectification. The paper indexed as P22 demonstrates this distinction with a 13.2 kV design using nine cascaded cells per phase and 1.2 kV SiC devices.

This example isolates one AC/DC power supply: 480 V three-phase AC at its input and 800 V DC at its output. It represents the conversion function moved into a power rack or power room in the following architecture drawings. The supply may contain multiple internal conversion stages. It is not a UPS AC-to-DC-to-AC path or a model of the whole data center.

Before this example’s 480 V AC input, a conventional transformer steps medium-voltage AC down and provides galvanic isolation. Lower AC voltage reduces the voltage stress handled by the following power electronics. The transformer’s own losses are outside the one-power-supply calculation shown here.

The controlled AC/DC supply establishes the 800 V DC output; a simple rectifier is not a voltage-independent route to 800 V. SemiAnalysis’s Phase 3 example uses 415 V AC after conventional step-down. This numerical example retains 480 V AC; neither is a universal required input voltage.

A conventional transformer changes AC voltage; it does not rectify. There is no universal 10 kV ceiling on rectification. Cascaded converter cells can share medium-voltage stress among lower-voltage semiconductors. An SST is an alternative architecture that combines electronic stages with high-frequency isolation, not a prerequisite for an 800 V DC bus. See D04, “Why step down before rectifying?”, for the device-rating distinction.

Conversion changes voltage or electrical form with real components. Current through semiconductor on-resistance, winding resistance and diode drops dissipates power. Switching transitions dissipate energy as current and voltage overlap; repeating those transitions adds average loss. Magnetic components also dissipate power. The electronic converter’s controllers and gate drivers draw power; fans or pumps add auxiliary load where fitted. The balance depends on converter topology, device choices, voltage, load, switching frequency, temperature and operating mode.

Efficiency η is useful output power divided by input power. At a fixed output, P_loss = P_out × (1/η − 1). The slide assumes 98% efficiency solely to demonstrate the calculation: 100/0.98 = 102.0408 kW input, so loss is 2.0408 kW. It is not the efficiency of the pictured UPS or a measured advantage of AC or DC distribution.

To compare architectures, read the actual equipment efficiency curves at the required loading and mode, then sum losses along the complete path. Fewer conversion boxes or lower conductor heat alone does not establish lower total facility input.
steps.heat_headline: The electronic AC/DC converter loses some input power as heat.

steps.title: AC enters the compute rack and is converted to DC inside it.
steps.headline: AC enters the compute rack and is converted to DC inside it.
notes: Follow facility AC into the compute rack; locate conversion, then device regulation.
Conversion equipment occupies rack space that could otherwise support compute.
Conceptual placement: protection, grounding and other required equipment omitted.
steps.cue: Trace the incoming supply to the devices; point out the space occupied by conversion.
explanation: A simplified AC-to-rack arrangement brings AC to the compute rack, converts it to DC there, and regulates voltage again near the devices. Conversion equipment occupies rack space that could otherwise serve other functions.
The functional drawing omits protection, grounding and other required equipment. It locates conversion without specifying a buildable installation.

These are representative architecture choices, consistent with NVIDIA’s dated AC, hybrid and native-DC roadmap. They are not three required stages that every facility must pass through; actual deployments can combine approaches.
This is the conventional AC baseline, not SemiAnalysis Phase 1. The later labels refer to the article’s forecast adoption phases, which are unrelated to the three electrical phases of an AC waveform.

steps.title: A nearby power rack converts AC to DC, freeing space inside the compute rack.
steps.headline: A nearby power rack converts AC to DC, freeing space inside the compute rack.
notes: Move conversion beside the compute rack; DC begins after the sidecar converter.
Compute-rack space released; sidecar still needs hall space, cooling and service access.
Upstream AC constraints and final low-voltage device regulation remain.
SemiAnalysis forecasts Phase 1 in 2026/27 and Phase 2 in 2027/28. Both use an AC-fed power rack; DC/DC conversion moves from a rack shelf in Phase 1 onto the blade in Phase 2.
steps.cue: Move the converter; ask which space is freed and which space is now occupied.
explanation: A sidecar arrangement keeps upstream AC but places AC-to-DC conversion in nearby equipment. The 800 V DC segment begins after that conversion.

A sidecar can free compute-rack space while occupying space nearby. It does not by itself establish net hall-space savings. The converter still needs cooling and service access; upstream AC limits and final device regulation remain.

These are representative architecture choices, consistent with NVIDIA’s dated AC, hybrid and native-DC roadmap. They are not three required stages that every facility must pass through; actual deployments can combine approaches.

In the May 26, 2026 SemiAnalysis forecast, Phase 1 (2026/2027) and Phase 2 (2027/2028) both use near-rack conversion. The important internal distinction is where 800 V is stepped down: a rack shelf in Phase 1 versus on-blade conversion in Phase 2. This drawing groups their shared AC-fed sidecar arrangement; it does not depict identical rack internals. Backup is omitted from these placement drawings: the article discusses DC-coupled batteries and supercapacitors replacing central UPS functions, while also expecting some operators to retain a central UPS. The forecast does not imply one universal backup topology.

steps.title: Upstream conversion lets 800 V DC run through the data hall.
steps.headline: Upstream conversion lets 800 V DC run through the data hall.
notes: Move conversion into a power room → longer DC distribution segment.
Selected equipment leaves the hall; its footprint and supporting services move elsewhere.
Final device regulation remains; conceptual placement does not establish installed results or total footprint savings.
NVIDIA’s 54 V DC rack comparison uses another boundary; our numerical baseline stays 480 V AC.
SemiAnalysis Phase 3: late 2028/2029, with conventional step-down to 415 V AC before the upstream rectifier. Our separate numerical example uses 480 V AC. This drawing does not show an SST.
steps.cue: Trace where DC begins; compare the released hall space with the new power-room footprint.
explanation: Moving conversion into a power room extends the DC distribution segment and can free hall space occupied by selected conversion equipment. The equipment still has a footprint and supporting requirements at its new location.
NVIDIA also describes a separate 54 V DC rack-distribution constraint. Our numerical baseline remains the 480 V AC feeder. Final low-voltage device conversion remains necessary in both cases.
These conceptual diagrams compare placement; they do not establish installed results, total-footprint savings or an efficiency ranking.

These are representative architecture choices, consistent with NVIDIA’s dated AC, hybrid and native-DC roadmap. They are not three required stages that every facility must pass through; actual deployments can combine approaches.

SemiAnalysis forecasts Phase 3 for late 2028/2029: conventional step-down followed by a low-voltage AC-to-800 V DC rectifier upstream. Its separate Phase 4 concerns medium-voltage input and SSTs; the heading says after 2029 while its body says early 2029, so no single exact date is adopted for that phase. These are dated forecasts, not confirmed installation dates.

learning_contract.driving_question: How can denser racks use less distribution copper and less space for power conversion?
learning_contract.fixed_boundary: 100 kW average power received throughout the electrical primer and feeder comparison. The converter-loss illustration has a separate 100 kW output boundary.
learning_contract.changed_variable: 480 V three-phase AC versus 800 V two-wire DC, then conversion placement.
learning_contract.primary_payoff: Explain copper quantity and equipment placement before evaluating energy savings.
learning_contract.misconception: Alternating current means no net energy delivery; three conductors triple the load; fewer conductors means less current; or 800 V alone guarantees usable extra capacity.
learning_contract.closing_question: What copper is removed, what conversion equipment moves, and which space is freed by the chosen 800 V architecture?
